::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Is $|\sin x|$ differentiable at $2k\pi$ for $k \in \mathbb N$?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2025121/is-sin-x-differentiable-at-2k-pi-for-k-in-mathbb-n), asked by [Omar Qasem](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/286661/omar-qasem) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2016-11-22; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> Just to check since I'm not sure about this one:
>
> > Is $|\sin x|$ differentiable at $2k\pi$ for $k \in \mathbb N$?
>
> If so then does the derivative at $2k \pi$ equal zero?
:::

Since $f$ is periodic with period $2\pi$, it suffices to show $f$ is not differentiable at $0$.  It's easiest to do this from the definition.

If $0 < h < \pi$, then 
$$\frac{f(0+h)-f(0)}{h} = \frac{|\sin(h)|}{h} = \frac{\sin(h)}{h} \to 1$$
as $h\to 0^+$.  On the other hand, if $-\pi < h < 0$, then 
$$\frac{f(0+h)-f(0)}{h} = \frac{|\sin(h)|}{h} = \frac{-\sin(h)}{h} \to -1$$
as $h\to 0^-$.  Since $\lim_{h\to 0} \frac{f(0+h)-f(0)}{h}$ does not exist, $f$ is not differentiable at $0$.
